tagline.text: A 37-figure bronze tribute to the 1986 EDSA Revolution in Quezon City

location.label: Location
location.text: Camp Aguinaldo, Quezon City, at the corner of EDSA and White Plains Avenue

children.text: The People Power Monument is a bronze sculpture about 18 m tall, built at the corner of EDSA and White Plains Avenue to commemorate the 1986 EDSA Revolution. Thirty-seven figures are stacked in a pyramid, making it a good short stop for a look back at a turning point in Philippine democracy.

The People Power Monument, known in Filipino as Monumento ng Lakas ng Bayan, is a sculpted commemorative tower. It stands at the corner of EDSA (Epifanio de los Santos Avenue) and White Plains Avenue in Barangay Camp Aguinaldo, Quezon City, and is about
tall. The sculptor was Eduardo Castrillo, and the monument is generally said to have opened to the public in 1993. It lies about
0.9km
in a straight line from the EDSA Shrine on the same avenue, so many visitors see the two together.

The monument commemorates the People Power Revolution, which unfolded along EDSA from February 22 to 25, 1986. Opposition leader Ninoy Aquino was assassinated on August 21, 1983, as he returned from exile at Manila's airport, and the snap presidential election of February 7, 1986 was followed by disputes over fraud. More than two million civilians then gathered on the streets in front of the military camps, and the Marcos family left for Hawaii, ending about 20 years of rule. Corazon Aquino was inaugurated as the 11th president. Because power changed hands without large-scale bloodshed, the event is also called the Bloodless Revolution (though some counts put the death toll at 13 to 18), and the Yellow Revolution after the yellow ribbons. In 2003, the radio broadcasts of the revolution were inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World International Register. The event is often cited not only in the Philippines but in the world history of democratization.

The sculpture is built as a pyramid. According to Wikipedia, it consists of 37 figures representing different sectors of Philippine society. On the bottom tier are people with linked arms, and a figure identified as Ninoy Aquino points toward the EDSA Shrine and Ortigas. The middle tier includes a musician, a mother holding an infant, a person with a "Laban" (fight) sign, and priests and nuns. At the top, a female figure with raised arms and unchained shackles stands in front of a large flag. This top figure, symbolizing freedom, is the face of the monument. EDSA is named after Epifanio de los Santos, a historian and jurist. Republic Act No. 2140 renamed the old Highway 54 on April 7, 1959, and the avenue is about

long. The MRT-3 elevated train runs along it, and Camp Aguinaldo and Camp Crame face each other across it. A look at the map makes it easy to see why the revolution happened on this road. For travelers short on time, a half day combining the monument and the shrine is the most rewarding choice.

The monument was long maintained by a private group, the Spirit of EDSA Foundation. Under Executive Order No. 47 of 2017, the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) took over its management, and the handover was formally made on February 25, 2018, the 32nd anniversary of the revolution. Planning and running the annual commemorations in February is understood to remain with the EDSA People Power Commission. Management and event arrangements can change, so check the latest announcements before you visit.

The heart of the monument is its 37 bronze figures representing every layer of Philippine society. Looking up from close range, you can pick out linked-arm citizens, a musician, a mother with her child, and priests and nuns, tier by tier. Moving your eyes up one level at a time takes only
10–15 minutes

blocks.title: The Lady of Freedom and the flag

children.text: At the very top, a female figure raises both arms with her shackles broken, and a large flag and flagpole rise behind her. The scene condenses the moment freedom was regained into a single image. Her outline is clearest at dusk, when the light falls at an angle.

One figure on the bottom tier is identified as Ninoy Aquino, and his hand points toward the EDSA Shrine and Ortigas. If you line the direction up with a map, the flow of the road where citizens gathered during the revolution makes sense.

On the middle tier, a figure holds a "Laban" sign. It carries into sculpture a slogan widely used in the anti-dictatorship movement of the 1980s, and it is a small thrill to see in person a sign you may know from Philippine history books.

blocks.title: The information marker and NHCP plaque

children.text: The monument is understood to carry an NHCP marker, along with text explaining the meaning of the event. The text is in Filipino and English and helps you check dates and names. The location and content of the markers can change.

blocks.title: Pair it with the EDSA Shrine

children.text: The EDSA Shrine stands about
0.9km

from the monument in a straight line. It is a church of the Virgin Mary dedicated on December 15, 1989, with a bronze statue called Our Lady of EDSA, Queen of Peace. Visiting both gives the story of the revolution more depth.

This is still a place where people gather. A rally against the burial of Marcos was held here in November 2016, and the "Trillion Peso March" against corruption took place on September 21, 2025. If an event falls on your visit date, traffic will back up, so check in advance.
Get off at MRT-3 Santolan-Annapolis station and head along EDSA. A taxi or Grab is easiest for the stretch to the White Plains Avenue corner.
On arrival, start from the bottom tier and move slowly. Check the linked-arm citizens and the direction in which the figure identified as Ninoy Aquino points.
Look for the musician, the mother with an infant, the "Laban" sign, and the priests and nuns on the middle tier. Look up at the top figure and the flag, and take photos.
Read the information marker and the NHCP plaque, and go over the dates and places of the revolution once more.
The monument stands at a busy intersection corner with heavy traffic. When taking photos, be careful not to step back toward the road.
Look around the People Power Monument.
Take a taxi or Grab to the EDSA Shrine. It is about
0.9km
in a straight line, but the travel time varies greatly with traffic.
At the EDSA Shrine, see the bronze statue of Our Lady of EDSA, Queen of Peace, and the church interior. Check the shrine's official notices for Mass times.
Finish with lunch at a mall or restaurant in the Ortigas Center area.
From the provinces or overseas, land at Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL). From the airport to the monument, go by taxi or Grab, and
allow plenty of time
because the trip varies greatly with traffic.
If you want to continue by MRT-3 from the airport, first check where to transfer in the city.
MRT-3 is an elevated train running along EDSA from North Avenue to Taft Avenue.

Santolan-Annapolis station and Ortigas station are the stations near the monument. From the station, walk or take a short taxi or jeepney ride. Judge the walking distance and safety by conditions on the day.
Train hours and fares change. Check the latest MRT-3 notices before you go.
Search for "People Power Monument" or "EDSA corner White Plains Avenue" and you will find it right away on a map app.
The monument is at an intersection corner, so getting in and out of a vehicle may not be easy. Ask the driver for a safe place to drop you off.
City buses run along EDSA, and you can take one from the Santolan side toward White Plains.
Routes and stops can change, so check on the spot.
The monument is outdoors by the roadside, so it is fully exposed to the weather. Visiting in the dry season,
November–May
, lets you look around without worrying about rain.
The most meaningful time of year is around the revolution anniversary,
February 25
. Ceremonies and wreath-laying take place then, but traffic is heavy and crowds are large.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: A good time for photos and easy walking. Commemorations are held around February 25.
The midday sun is strong. Choose morning or dusk.
Rainy season, with showers and possible flooding
Rain snarls traffic and makes the area around the monument muddy. Watch for typhoon news.

There is almost no lodging right next to the monument. The nearby Ortigas Center and Quezon City areas have many hotels and serviced residences, which suit travelers planning to see the EDSA Shrine and the monument together. Check the distance and transport on a map app before you book.
Meals are easiest at the malls and food courts of the Ortigas Center. A Filipino-style meal costs about
, and there are also Korean and Japanese restaurants. Street vendors and convenience stores near the monument sell water and snacks.
The monument is at a major road intersection, so always cross using signals, footbridges, and crosswalks.
Photos taken in the early morning or at dusk show the outlines of the sculpture clearly.
Seeing the EDSA Shrine on the same day saves time. The shrine's highlight is its bronze statue of the Virgin Mary.
Around the revolution anniversary (February 25) there are wreath-laying ceremonies and citizen gatherings that add to what you can see, but EDSA traffic is extremely congested.
When booking a Grab, enter both "People Power Monument" and "White Plains Avenue" on the map so the driver does not get confused about where to go.
Knowing the history makes the visit far more interesting. Just learning the order of the 1983 assassination of Ninoy, the events of February 22–25, 1986, and Corazon Aquino's inauguration is enough.
The monument stands at a busy corner where EDSA meets White Plains Avenue, so watch the traffic whenever you take photos or cross.
On days with rallies or events, roads are closed or jammed. Check the news before you go.
In crowded places, watch for pickpockets and phone snatchers, and carry your bag in front of you.
Facilities and information boards around the monument can change. Check the latest notices for operation and management information.

The Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines is understood to have stated that the revolution-related sculpture and monument are protected by copyright, so check in advance before any commercial shooting.
It is a politically sensitive subject. When talking with locals, listen rather than pushing your own opinions.
A large business and shopping district next to the EDSA Shrine. It is about
10–20 minutes
by car from the monument and a good place for meals and lodging.
A large park and memorial tower in Quezon City. It is
20–40 minutes
away by taxi and a good way to continue your Quezon City sightseeing.
A church of the Virgin Mary about
0.9km
in a straight line from the monument. It was dedicated on December 15, 1989, and was declared a National Shrine in January 2025.

Two military camps facing each other across EDSA. During the revolution, military officers took control of them and crowds gathered at their gates. They are military facilities, so entry inside is restricted.
